reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours; Berek & Novak's Gynecology
clinicalPearls: The commonest malignant ovarian sex-cord stromal tumour; oestrogen production drives much of the clinical picture, causing post-menopausal bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia or frank endometrial carcinoma in adults, and isosexual precocious puberty in the juvenile form.

Two clinicopathological types exist: the adult type (about 95 per cent) presenting in peri- and post-menopausal women, and the juvenile type presenting in children and young women, distinguished by histology and behaviour rather than simply by age.

A somatic FOXL2 missense mutation (C134W) is present in the great majority of adult-type tumours and is a useful diagnostic marker; juvenile-type tumours usually lack it and may harbour other alterations.
Inhibin (particularly inhibin B) and anti-Mullerian hormone are valuable serum markers for diagnosis and, importantly, for detecting recurrence during long-term follow-up.

Characteristic histology shows Call-Exner bodies, coffee-bean grooved nuclei, and diffuse, trabecular, insular or microfollicular growth patterns; immunohistochemistry is positive for inhibin, calretinin, SF-1 and FOXL2.
Most present at an early, confined stage, and surgery is the mainstay; fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is reasonable in young women with disease apparently limited to one ovary.
Late recurrence is characteristic and may occur many years or even decades after initial treatment, mandating prolonged surveillance rather than a fixed short follow-up window.
Because oestrogen excess is common, endometrial sampling is essential at diagnosis to exclude concurrent hyperplasia or carcinoma of the endometrium.
reference.pathophysiology: Granulosa cell tumours arise from the granulosa cells of the ovarian follicle, part of the sex-cord stromal compartment, often in association with theca cells and fibroblasts. Neoplastic granulosa cells retain the capacity for steroidogenesis and typically secrete oestrogens (and inhibin and anti-Mullerian hormone), producing the hyperoestrogenic clinical syndrome. In the adult type, a recurrent somatic FOXL2 point mutation disrupts a transcription factor essential to granulosa cell identity and folliculogenesis, and is regarded as a driver event. The juvenile type shows different molecular alterations, including changes in the AKT/PI3K and Gs-alpha signalling pathways, correlating with its distinct morphology of luxuriant follicle formation and more mitotically active, atypical cells. Tumours are generally indolent and low-grade, but their steroid output and their tendency to spread locally and recur late reflect ongoing hormonally active, slowly proliferating clones.
additionalDifferentials: diffuse or poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ovary
small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcaemic type
metastatic breast carcinoma to the ovary
additionalInvestigations: serum inhibin B and anti-Mullerian hormone
endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopic sampling to assess the endometrium
contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of abdomen and pelvis for staging
FOXL2 mutation analysis on tumour tissue
redFlags: post-menopausal bleeding with an adnexal mass suggesting concurrent endometrial pathology
acute abdomen from tumour rupture with haemoperitoneum
rapidly enlarging mass or ascites suggesting higher-stage or aggressive disease
recurrent disease presenting years after treatment with rising inhibin or anti-Mullerian hormone
signs of virilisation raising concern for an alternative or mixed steroidogenic tumour
reference.prognosis: Overall prognosis is favourable because most adult-type tumours present at an early stage and behave indolently, but late relapse is characteristic and long-term survival falls with advanced stage or recurrence. The juvenile type is usually cured when confined to the ovary, though the rare advanced cases can behave aggressively.
pitfalls: Assuming a benign course and stopping surveillance early, when recurrence can appear decades later.
Failing to sample the endometrium and missing concurrent hyperplasia or carcinoma driven by oestrogen excess.
Mistaking the tumour for a poorly differentiated carcinoma or thecoma on limited sampling without inhibin, calretinin and FOXL2 studies.
Over-relying on any single tumour marker; inhibin and anti-Mullerian hormone are complementary and neither is perfectly sensitive.
Attributing virilisation to a granulosa cell tumour, which is usually oestrogenic, and overlooking a Sertoli-Leydig or steroid cell tumour.

management: Surgery is the definitive treatment, with staging surgery and salpingo-oophorectomy, and fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy appropriate for young women with apparently unilateral confined disease
Evaluate the endometrium and treat oestrogen-driven hyperplasia or frank endometrial carcinoma
Offer platinum-based adjuvant chemotherapy for advanced-stage or incompletely resected tumours
Follow up long term with serum inhibin B and anti-Mullerian hormone, reflecting the characteristic late relapse
Treat relapse with secondary cytoreductive surgery, chemotherapy or hormonal agents such as aromatase inhibitors
Confirm diagnosis with inhibin, calretinin, SF-1 and FOXL2 markers and manage within a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team
